_note: Cambridge B2 First — Reading and Use of English, Part 1 (multiple-choice cloze). Eight gaps plus a worked example, four options each, one text. Built to hold many tests: everything specific to one text lives inside its own entry in `tests`, so adding a second is appending an object and changing nothing else. The `why` field on each question is the teaching — Part 1 is decided by collocation, dependent preposition and fixed phrase far more often than by meaning, and a student who only sees the right answer learns the answer rather than the reason.
title: Reading and Use of English — Part 1
timing: The whole paper is 1 hour 15 minutes. Part 1 is worth 8 marks of 52.
rubric: For questions 1–8, read the text below and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap. There is an example at the beginning (0).

tests.title: Home and abroad
tests._text: Paragraphs carry {0} … {8} where the gaps fall. Placeholders are numbered, not positional, so a renderer never has to count them and a gap can be re-ordered without silently changing which question it belongs to.
text: After a short time living in a foreign country, I noticed conversations with locals assumed a {0} pattern. There were standard answers to the usual questions. Most questions caused little {1} — it was rather like dancing, where both partners know how to avoid {2} on each other's toes.

But, 'When are you going home?' was a question I {3} to answer, whenever I {4} my life and the direction it seemed to be {5}. In the last ten years, I had lived in a dozen countries. And I had travelled through dozens more; usually in {6} of a purpose or a person; occasionally to see the attractions.

This kind of travel is not {7} wandering, but is the extensive exploration of a wide {8} of cultures. However, it doesn't allow you to put down roots. At the back of your mind, though, is the idea of home, the place you came from.

example.why: A pattern you can foresee is a predictable one. 'Steady' describes a rate that does not change, 'main' a thing's chief part, and 'respectable' is about esteem — none of them says foreseeable.

questions.why: 'Cause trouble' is the fixed pair. The other three are things you cause far less naturally, and 'little trouble' is the idiomatic way to say something was easy.

distractors.puzzle: a puzzle is something to solve, not something a question causes
distractors.obstacle: an obstacle is placed in your way; questions do not cause them
distractors.barrier: a barrier blocks — too strong, and it collocates with 'language', not 'cause'

questions.why: 'Step on someone's toes' is the idiom, here used literally of dancing and figuratively of conversation at the same time. The idiom admits no substitute.

distractors.touching: the right general sense, but the fixed phrase is not 'touching on toes'
distractors.moving: moving on someone's toes is not English
distractors.walking: you walk on a floor, not on toes

questions.why: 'Struggle to do something' means to find it hard. Of the four, only 'struggled' takes a to-infinitive with this meaning.

distractors.worked: 'worked to answer' needs a purpose, not a difficulty
distractors.competed: you compete with someone, not to answer a question

questions.why: The gap is followed directly by an object — 'my life'. 'Consider' takes one; 'think' and 'reflect' need 'about' and 'on'. This is a preposition question wearing a vocabulary question's clothes.

distractors.believed: you believe a proposition, not a life

questions.why: A direction is something a life or a journey takes. 'Take a direction' is the pair; the others are all things done to a direction from outside.

distractors.making: you make a decision, not a direction
distractors.finding: possible in isolation, but the subject is the life itself, which takes rather than finds
distractors.seeking: seeking a direction is deliberate; the sentence describes drift

questions.why: 'In search of' is fixed. Note how close the trap is: 'in sight of' is also a real phrase, but it means near enough to see, not looking for.

distractors.sight: 'in sight of' is real English with the wrong meaning — the sharpest distractor here
distractors.inquiry: an inquiry is a formal investigation

questions.why: The sentence contrasts this travel with wandering that has no purpose, and 'aimless' is exactly purposeless. The paragraph then supplies the contrast: extensive exploration.

distractors.unreasonable: about fairness or sense, not about purpose
distractors.indefinite: about duration or vagueness, not aim

questions.why: 'A wide variety of' is the set phrase. 'Wide' fixes it — you can have a wide variety and a wide range, but not a wide difference or a wide order.

distractors.difference: 'a wide difference' is not idiomatic; differences are between two things
distractors.arrangement: an arrangement is a plan or a layout
distractors.order: 'in order of' exists, but 'a wide order of cultures' does not
